Ben Hogan. An American professional golfer whose technical precision and fierce competitiveness made him one of the sport's greatest players of the mid-twentieth century. Despite a career nearly ended by a severe automobile accident in 1949, he won 9 major championships and became renowned for his mechanical perfection and mental toughness.

He won 9 major championships: 4 US Opens in 1948, 1950, 1951, and 1953, 2 Masters in 1951 and 1953, 2 PGA Championships in 1946 and 1948, and 1 Open Championship in 1953. In February 1949, he suffered a nearly fatal car crash that left him with serious injuries; doctors doubted he would ever walk normally again. But he returned to competition 11 months after the accident and won the US Open in 1950, demonstrating extraordinary physical and psychological resilience.

Hogan was famous for his meticulous swing technique and obsessive practice habits. He authored Five Lessons: The Modern Fundamentals of Golf, a foundational instructional text that shaped how the game was taught. In 1953, he won three major championships—the Masters, the US Open, and The Open Championship—nearly capturing the Grand Slam and missing only the PGA Championship due to scheduling. Known as Bantam Ben for his small stature at five feet eight inches, he proved that size was irrelevant to dominance in golf. He pioneered the modern approach to golf instruction through technical analysis and filmed demonstrations.
